source.title: Do Language Models Encode Semantic Relations? Probing and Sparse Feature Analysis

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some table layout is flattened, but the reported model, relation, and metric groupings are recoverable; the text is not cut off or garbled in a way that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether SAE-selected sparse features in language models carry relation-specific information by injecting or ablating them and measuring probe-level effects. This is a different method and subject from toy-model superposition; it does not test overlapping directions or capacity competition.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition in related work but does not test its toy-model claims, overcomplete feature geometry, or neuron-level capacity account. Rows below cover the SAE-feature interventions bearing on V4. Dense probing and cosine-similarity results do not measure sparse feature recovery; the top-k sweep is used to select an intervention budget, not reported as a finding about the claim.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained SAELens SAEs as a tool. It ranks SAE latents by the coefficients of a linear probe, then ablates or injects them and measures changes in that same probe's margin and predictions, not the model's outputs. This shows its own probe-plus-SAE method is manipulable. It does not test whether models spread features across neurons, whether an SAE recovers sparse features the model actually uses, or anything about superposition geometry or capacity. The 'diffuse' findings refer to spread across layers, not across neurons. Superposition is cited only in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors also conclude that relation signals are diffuse across mid-layers and strongest in post-residual and MLP streams. They find a stable difficulty ordering (antonymy easiest, synonymy hardest) and a hypernymy/hyponymy directional asymmetry. They limit their causal claims to probe-level effects.
record.recipe_differences: Uses WordNet relation probes, pretrained SAEs, and SAE-feature injection/ablation to measure probe-level semantic logit and prediction changes; it does not reproduce toy-network superposition experiments or measure overlap geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Model scale changes the magnitude and reliability of SAE intervention effects. In Llama 3.1, prompt format changes reported sufficiency and necessity measures.

fits_no_version.finding: A linear probe's relation predictions shift when its top-coefficient SAE latents are injected or ablated. Effects are strong on Llama 3.1 8B (ΔFR 0.66–0.79, DR 0.24–0.62) and weak on Pythia-70M and GPT-2. Random latents give below 10% of the effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Probe-ranked SAE latents carry relation-specific, probe-level causal signal, and its strength grows with model scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Hypernymy shows high sufficiency but low necessity, while hyponymy is high on both. The authors read this as redundant versus compact encoding.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hierarchical relations show a directional asymmetry in how SAE latents encode them.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation
record.problems: Evidence is limited to three base decoder-only models, WordNet English lexical relations, and probe-level outcomes; the authors do not establish effects on generated model outputs. Behavioral flip/drop rates have no uncertainty intervals reported in the tables. The paper notes that patching can exaggerate effects under nonlinear feature interactions. Its conclusion that features are redundant or compact is an interpretation of probe-level measures, not a direct measurement of superposition geometry.
record.rows_left_out: Did not catalog dense linear-probe accuracy, cosine similarity, word-order reversal accuracy, or the top-k selection sweep: these do not directly measure SAE sparse-feature recovery for V4. Table 6 mean and peak dense-probe accuracies are likewise omitted; its SAE-guided flip/drop results are included.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity transition or feature geometry.
No neuron polysemanticity or capacity-allocation analysis.
No result on alternative causes of polysemanticity.

SAEs are used, not tested. There is no measure of features spread across neurons, SAE reconstruction or fidelity, or whether the latents are features the model uses (effects are on an external probe only).
No test of SAE completeness, stability or canonicity.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. SAEs are a tool here, and every intervention outcome is read from a linear probe rather than from model outputs, so no row bears on V4. The record's Table 5 drop-rate values for Pythia and GPT-2 appear swapped: the prose says Pythia DR ≤0.21 and GPT-2 DR ≤0.14. Pythia DR should likely be 0.14/0.21/0.14/0.20 and GPT-2 DR 0.05/0.13/0.04/0.14. Table 4 and the remaining values match the text.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, overcomplete sparse feature sets, overlapping directions, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry are tested.
No test of neuron polysemanticity as a capacity consequence, dedicated dimensions for important features, or features sharing dimensions.
The paper mentions polysemanticity in related work but reports no result about alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.

Tests SAE-selected features associated with semantic-relation probe signals in three models, not whether features are spread across neurons or whether this generalizes beyond these relations, models, prompts, and probe-level measures.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units of model representation.
Does not test whether the represented features are one-dimensional directions or compare them with multidimensional features.
